claim: The periaqueductal grey (PAG) plays a pivotal role in fear learning.
source: The pivotal role of the periaqueductal grey (PAG) in fear learning is reinforced by the identification of neurons in male rat ventrolateral PAG (vlPAG) that encode fear memory through signalling the onset and offset of an auditory-conditioned stimulus during presentation of the unreinforced conditioned tone (CS+) during retrieval.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about the PAG's role, supported by the experimental findings described in the manuscript.

claim: Neurons in male rat ventrolateral PAG (vlPAG) encode fear memory through signalling the onset and offset of an auditory-conditioned stimulus during presentation of the unreinforced conditioned tone (CS+) during retrieval.
source: The pivotal role of the periaqueductal grey (PAG) in fear learning is reinforced by the identification of neurons in male rat ventrolateral PAG (vlPAG) that encode fear memory through signalling the onset and offset of an auditory-conditioned stimulus during presentation of the unreinforced conditioned tone (CS+) during retrieval.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the electrophysiological recordings and data analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: Some vlPAG units only display CS+ onset or offset responses.
source: Some units only display CS+ onset or offset responses, and the two signals differ in extinction sensitivity, suggesting that they are independent of each other.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing that 3/29 units (10.3%) only responded to CS+ onset and 5/29 units only responded to CS+ offset (17.3%).

claim: CS+ onset and offset signals differ in extinction sensitivity, suggesting that they are independent of each other.
source: Some units only display CS+ onset or offset responses, and the two signals differ in extinction sensitivity, suggesting that they are independent of each other.
evidence: This is supported by data showing different patterns of extinction for onset versus offset responses, as detailed in Figure 2 and related text.

claim: Reversible inactivation of the medial cerebellar nucleus (MCN) during fear consolidation leads to disruption of the temporal precision of vlPAG offset, but not onset responses to CS+ during subsequent retrieval.
source: In addition, understanding cerebellar contributions to survival circuits is advanced by the discovery that (i) reversible inactivation of the medial cerebellar nucleus (MCN) during fear consolidation leads in subsequent retrieval to (a) disruption of the temporal precision of vlPAG offset, but not onset responses to CS+
evidence: This is supported by muscimol inactivation experiments showing increased number and altered latency of peaks at CS+ offset but not onset (Figure 4).

claim: Reversible inactivation of the MCN during fear consolidation leads to an increase in duration of freezing behaviour during subsequent retrieval.
source: In addition, understanding cerebellar contributions to survival circuits is advanced by the discovery that (i) reversible inactivation of the medial cerebellar nucleus (MCN) during fear consolidation leads in subsequent retrieval to (a) disruption of the temporal precision of vlPAG offset, but not onset responses to CS+, and (b) an increase in duration of freezing behaviour.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing significantly longer freezing epochs in muscimol animals compared to controls (Figure 5C).

claim: Chemogenetic manipulation of the MCN-vlPAG projection during fear acquisition reduces the occurrence of fear-related ultrasonic vocalisations.
source: And (ii) chemogenetic manipulation of the MCN-vlPAG projection during fear acquisition (a) reduces the occurrence of fear-related ultrasonic vocalisations
evidence: This is supported by DREADD experiments showing a 36% reduction in USVs during the ITI in acquisition (Figure 6C).

claim: Chemogenetic manipulation of the MCN-vlPAG projection during fear acquisition slows the extinction rate of fear-related freezing during subsequent retrieval.
source: And (ii) chemogenetic manipulation of the MCN-vlPAG projection during fear acquisition (a) reduces the occurrence of fear-related ultrasonic vocalisations, and (b) during subsequent retrieval, slows the extinction rate of fear-related freezing.
evidence: This is supported by DREADD experiments showing significantly slower extinction rate during CS+ in DREADD animals (Figure 7C).

claim: The cerebellum is part of the survival network that regulates fear memory processes at multiple timescales and in multiple ways.
source: These findings show that the cerebellum is part of the survival network that regulates fear memory processes at multiple timescales and in multiple ways, raising the possibility that dysfunctional interactions in the cerebellar-survival network may underlie fear-related disorders and comorbidities.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the combined experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dysfunctional interactions in the cerebellar-survival network may underlie fear-related disorders and comorbidities.
source: These findings show that the cerebellum is part of the survival network that regulates fear memory processes at multiple timescales and in multiple ways, raising the possibility that dysfunctional interactions in the cerebellar-survival network may underlie fear-related disorders and comorbidities.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings and their potential clinical implications.

claim: Fear-evoked freezing is mediated by neurons in the ventrolateral sector of the PAG (vlPAG).
source: Of particular relevance to the current study, fear-evoked freezing is mediated by neurons in its ventrolateral sector (vlPAG; Vianna et al., 2001; Walker and Carrive, 2003; Tovote et al., 2016; Watson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Fear-related behaviours coordinated by the PAG extend to the expression of 22 kHz ultrasonic vocalisations (USVs).
source: Fear-related behaviours coordinated by the PAG also extend to the expression of 22 kHz ultrasonic vocalisations (USVs; Kim et al., 2013; Ouda et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fear-related behaviours coordinated by the PAG include risk assessment activity such as rearing.
source: Fear-related behaviours coordinated by the PAG also extend to the expression of 22 kHz ultrasonic vocalisations (USVs; Kim et al., 2013; Ouda et al., 2016) and risk assessment activity such as rearing (Sandner et al., 1987; Clelland et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Neurons in vlPAG encode associatively conditioned fear memory at a cellular level.
source: Furthermore, at a cellular level, electrophysiological studies have found that neurons in vlPAG encode associatively conditioned fear memory (Watson et al., 2016; Wright et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: Inactivation of vermal cerebellar cortex (lobules IV–VIII) or the medial cerebellar nucleus leads to deficits in fear-related behaviours such as context-conditioned bradycardia.
source: However, there is good evidence in cats and rodents that vermal regions of the cerebellum contribute to motor and autonomic components of defensive states: inactivation of vermal cerebellar cortex (lobules IV–VIII), or one of its main output nuclei (medial cerebellar nucleus [MCN], aka fastigial nucleus), leads to deficits in fear-related behaviours such as context-conditioned bradycardia (Supple and Leaton, 1990)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Inactivation of vermal cerebellar cortex or MCN leads to deficits in the expression of innate fear.
source: inactivation of vermal cerebellar cortex (lobules IV–VIII), or one of its main output nuclei (medial cerebellar nucleus [MCN], aka fastigial nucleus), leads to deficits in fear-related behaviours such as context-conditioned bradycardia (Supple and Leaton, 1990) the expression of innate fear (Supple et al., 1987; Koutsikou et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Inactivation of vermal cerebellar cortex or MCN leads to deficits in fear-conditioned freezing behaviour.
source: inactivation of vermal cerebellar cortex (lobules IV–VIII), or one of its main output nuclei (medial cerebellar nucleus [MCN], aka fastigial nucleus), leads to deficits in fear-related behaviours such as context-conditioned bradycardia (Supple and Leaton, 1990) the expression of innate fear (Supple et al., 1987; Koutsikou et al., 2014); and fear-conditioned freezing behaviour (Asdourian and Frerichs, 1970; Sacchetti et al., 2002; Sacchetti et al., 2005; Koutsikou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The emission of USVs has been related to cerebellar function.
source: In addition, the emission of USVs has been related to cerebellar function (Fujita et al., 2008; Fujita-Jimbo and Momoi, 2014; Toledo et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Inactivation of the cerebellar vermis during innate and conditioned fear unmasks risk assessment rearing behaviour.
source: and inactivation of the cerebellar vermis during innate and conditioned fear unmasks risk assessment rearing behaviour (Koutsikou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The cerebellum is reciprocally connected to many brain regions associated with survival networks.
source: The cerebellum is reciprocally connected to many brain regions associated with survival networks (Sacchetti et al., 2009; Strick et al., 2009; Apps and Strata, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In all mammalian species studied so far (cat, rabbit, rat, mouse, human), the cerebellum has interconnections with the vlPAG.
source: and in all mammalian species studied so far (cat, rabbit, rat, mouse, human), this includes interconnections with the vlPAG (Whiteside and Snider, 1953; Teune et al., 2000; Nisimaru et al., 2013; Koutsikou et al., 2014; Cacciola et al., 2019; Vaaga et al., 2020; Frontera et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research across multiple species.

claim: The cerebellar vermis and its output nucleus MCN are involved in the control of an integrated array of fear-related functions, including fear memory and fear-induced behaviours such as freezing and their extinction.
source: An emerging concept is that the cerebellar vermis and its output nucleus MCN are involved in the control of an integrated array of fear-related functions, including fear memory and fear-induced behaviours such as freezing and their extinction (Sacchetti et al., 2002; Sacchetti et al., 2005; Koutsikou et al., 2014; Utz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Deficits in extinction processes are thought to underlie psychological conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
source: Effects during retrieval and subsequent extinction of a fear-conditioned response are of particular interest because deficits in extinction processes are thought to underlie psychological conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Bremner et al., 1999; Herry et al., 2010; Milad and Quirk, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on PTSD.

claim: Deficits in extinction processes have been related to chronic pain phenotype.
source: deficits in extinction processes are thought to underlie psychological conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Bremner et al., 1999; Herry et al., 2010; Milad and Quirk, 2012) and have also been related to chronic pain phenotype (Ji et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A total of 32 vlPAG units were recorded during habituation from eight animals.
source: A total of 32 vlPAG units (obtained from eight animals) were recorded during habituation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data collected.

claim: During habituation, 75% (24/32 units) of vlPAG units were unresponsive to the unconditioned auditory tone.
source: The majority (75%, n = 24/32 units) were unresponsive to the unconditioned auditory tone
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis.

claim: During habituation, 6/32 vlPAG units responded to tone onset with an increase in firing rate.
source: the remainder responded (see Materials and methods for definition) to tone onset (either increasing, n = 6/32 units, or decreasing firing rate, n = 2/32 units)
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis.

claim: During habituation, 2/32 vlPAG units responded to tone onset with a decrease in firing rate.
source: the remainder responded (see Materials and methods for definition) to tone onset (either increasing, n = 6/32 units, or decreasing firing rate, n = 2/32 units)
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis.

claim: During habituation, 15.6% of vlPAG units also responded to tone offset.
source: and in some of these cases (15.6%) also to tone offset (either increasing 3/32 units or decreasing firing rate 2/32 units).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis.

claim: A total of 50 vlPAG units were recorded during acquisition from 10 animals.
source: We recorded the activity of 50 vlPAG units (obtained from 10 animals) during acquisition where the CS tone was paired with the unconditioned stimulus (US footshock at tone offset (Figure 1C)).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data collected.

claim: During acquisition, 18.5% of vlPAG units responded to CS onset.
source: Some of these units (18.5 %) responded to CS onset.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis.

claim: During acquisition, 20% of vlPAG units displayed an increase in firing rate following the US.
source: Following the US, 20% of the total also displayed an increase in firing rate which presumably reflects sensory afferent drive to the PAG as a result of the aversive peripheral stimulus (e.g. Sanders et al., 1980; Heinricher et al., 1987; Sharma et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis with interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The average increase in vlPAG unit activity following the US during acquisition was not statistically significant.
source: Across all recorded units, the average increase in activity following the US was not statistically significant (Figure 1C, z-score < 1.96).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of the experimental data, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: A total of 55 vlPAG units were recorded during retrieval and extinction from 10 animals.
source: During retrieval and extinction of the conditioned response, we recorded a total of 55 vlPAG units (obtained from 10 animals).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data collected.

claim: During retrieval, 29 units (52.7%, from n = 9 animals) displayed a transient increase in activity during presentation of the unreinforced CS+.
source: In retrieval, 29 units (52.7%, from n = 9 animals) displayed a transient increase in activity during presentation of the unreinforced conditioned stimulus (CS+, Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis, with reference to Figures 1D and E.

claim: Type 1 vlPAG units are defined as those displaying a transient increase in activity during presentation of the unreinforced CS+.
source: In keeping with a previous classification of PAG unit activity during fear-conditioned extinction training (Watson et al., 2016), these units are defined as type 1.
evidence: This is a definition based on previous research cited.

claim: Type 1 vlPAG units typically show a phasic increase in activity at CS+ onset and an additional phasic increase in activity at CS+ offset.
source: The pattern of response was typically a phasic increase in activity at CS+ onset, but an additional feature not previously reported for vlPAG units was a phasic increase in activity at CS+ offset (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental observations, with reference to Figures 1D and E.

claim: 21/29 type 1 units (72.4%) responded to both CS+ onset and CS+ offset.
source: A total of 21/29 type 1 units (72.4%) responded to both CS+ onset and CS+ offset
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis.

claim: 3/29 type 1 units (10.3%) only responded to CS+ onset.
source: while 3/29 units (10.3%) only responded to CS+ onset
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis.

claim: 5/29 type 1 units (17.3%) only responded to CS+ offset.
source: and 5/29 units only responded to CS+ offset (17.3%).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis.

claim: CS+ onset and offset responses may be mediated by separate mechanisms.
source: This raises the possibility that CS+ onset and offset responses may be mediated by separate mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that some units respond only to onset or only to offset.

claim: 22 vlPAG units (40%) recorded during early extinction demonstrated no significant change in firing rate and were defined as type 2.
source: Of the remainder of the sample of vlPAG units recorded in control animals during EE, 22 units (40%) demonstrated no significant change in firing rate and were therefore defined as type 2 (Watson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis with reference to previous classification.

claim: 4 vlPAG units (7%) responded to CS+ onset with a decrease in firing rate and were classed as type 4.
source: Four units (7%) responded to CS+ onset with a decrease in firing rate (two of these units also reduced their firing rate at CS+ offset) and therefore were classed as type 4.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis.

claim: No type 3 units (biphasic response) were observed during early extinction.
source: No type 3 units (biphasic response) were observed.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental observations.

claim: 75% (18/24 units) of type 1 onset units showed a significant reduction in responsiveness during extinction training.
source: The majority of type 1 onset units (75%, 18/24 units) and type 1 offset units (73%, 19/26 units) showed a significant reduction in responsiveness during extinction training, as measured by the integrated area of response during CS+ trials in EE versus late extinction (LE, Figure 2B and D, control, type 1 onset units: t(17) = 5.146, p<0.0001, n = 18, paired t-test
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of the experimental data, with reference to Figures 2B and D.

claim: 73% (19/26 units) of type 1 offset units showed a significant reduction in responsiveness during extinction training.
source: The majority of type 1 onset units (75%, 18/24 units) and type 1 offset units (73%, 19/26 units) showed a significant reduction in responsiveness during extinction training, as measured by the integrated area of response during CS+ trials in EE versus late extinction (LE, Figure 2B and D, control, type 1 onset units: t(17) = 5.146, p<0.0001, n = 18, paired t-test; type 1 offset units, Figure 2F and H: t(18) = 4.4, p=0.0003, n = 19, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of the experimental data, with reference to Figures 2F and H.

claim: For type 1 onset responses, the reduction in responsiveness during extinction was not evident for mean peak z-score.
source: For type 1 onset responses, this reduction was not evident for mean peak z-score (Figure 2E, decrease of 13.8% from EE to LE; t(17) = 1.344, p=0.197, n = 18, paired t-test)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of the experimental data, with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: For type 1 offset responses, the reduction in responsiveness during extinction was evident for mean peak z-score (67.0% decrease from EE to LE).
source: but was evident for type 1 offset responses (Figure 2I, decrease of 67.0% from EE to LE; t(18) = 2.354, p=0.0302, n = 19, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of the experimental data, with reference to Figure 2I.

claim: The distinction between onset and offset responses in extinction sensitivity provides additional evidence that they may be evoked by separate mechanisms.
source: This distinction between onset and offset responses provides additional evidence that they may be evoked by separate mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential extinction patterns observed for onset versus offset responses.

claim: In trace conditioning, type 4 offset units (those with reduced activity at CS+ offset) showed activity related to time of CS+ offset.
source: We also recorded six units with type 4 responses (those with reduced activity at CS+ offset) and in trace conditioning their activity was also related to time of CS+ offset (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental observations from trace conditioning experiments, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: There was no statistical difference in time to peak or trough of response for units recorded during control versus trace conditioning.
source: A comparison of time to peak or trough of response for all available units recorded during control versus trace conditioning showed no statistical difference (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E; t(25) = 1.76, p=0.091, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and trace conditioning data, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: vlPAG activity at CS+ offset signals the conditioned tone offset rather than a prediction of the timing of the US.
source: These results are therefore consistent with vlPAG activity signalling the conditioned tone offset rather than a prediction of the timing of the US.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the trace conditioning experiments showing that offset responses follow CS+ offset timing, not US timing.

claim: The ERP waveform duration and spike activity in vlPAG were broadly concomitant.
source: For vlPAG, we were able to compare the ERP waveform to the simultaneously recorded unit activity and found that field duration and spike activity were broadly concomitant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the comparison between ERP and unit activity data, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ERP recorded in the vlPAG at CS+ onset had a significantly shorter onset latency (6.5 ± 1.45 ms) than the ERP recorded in MCN (25.2 ± 4.05 ms).
source: The ERP recorded in the vlPAG at CS+ onset had a significantly shorter onset latency than the ERP recorded in the same animals in MCN (vlPAG onset 6.5 ± 1.45 ms; MCN onset 25.2 ± 4.05 ms, t(10) = 4.33, p=0.007, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of ERP latency data.

claim: At CS+ onset, latency to peak was not significantly different between vlPAG (58.5 ± 7.4 ms) and MCN (84.7 ± 11.46 ms).
source: However, latency to peak was not significantly different (PAG peak 58.5 ± 7.4 ms; MCN peak 84.7 ± 11.46 ms, t(5) = 1.418, p=0.215, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of ERP latency data.

claim: At CS+ offset, the ERP in the vlPAG was significantly shorter in latency (32 ± 5.2 ms) than the ERP in MCN (47.7 ± 3.3 ms).
source: At CS+ offset, the ERP in the vlPAG was also significantly shorter in latency than the ERP in MCN (vlPAG offset 32 ± 5.2 ms; MCN offset 47.7 ± 3.3 ms, t(5) = 2.991, p=0.0304; paired t-test)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of ERP latency data.

claim: At CS+ offset, latency to peak was similar between vlPAG (99 ± 6.4 ms) and MCN (100.7 ± 6.14 ms).
source: while latency to peak was similar (vlPAG peak 99 ± 6.4 ms; MCN peak 100.7 ± 6.14 ms, t(5) = 1.746, p=0.141, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of ERP latency data.

claim: The difference in onset latency between ERP responses recorded at CS+ onset and offset within vlPAG was statistically significant.
source: The difference in onset latency between ERP responses recorded at CS+ onset and offset within both vlPAG and MCN was statistically significant (vlPAG onset vs. offset, t(10) = 4.720, p=0.0008, unpaired t-test
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of ERP latency data.

claim: The difference in onset latency between ERP responses recorded at CS+ onset and offset within MCN was statistically significant.
source: The difference in onset latency between ERP responses recorded at CS+ onset and offset within both vlPAG and MCN was statistically significant (vlPAG onset vs. offset, t(10) = 4.720, p=0.0008, unpaired t-test; MCN onset vs. offset, t(10) = 4.319, p=0.0015, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of ERP latency data.

claim: Both MCN and vlPAG receive auditory inputs that convey information about conditioned tone onset and offset.
source: These findings indicate that both MCN and vlPAG receive auditory inputs that convey information about conditioned tone onset and offset.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ERP data showing responses to both tone onset and offset in both structures.

claim: The difference in latency between ERP responses at CS+ onset compared to CS+ offset within each structure suggests that they are likely to be generated by different neural pathways.
source: However, the difference in latency between ERP responses recorded at CS+ onset compared to CS+ offset within each structure suggests that they are also likely to be generated by different neural pathways.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed differences in ERP latencies.

claim: During extinction training, the peak-to-peak amplitude of the ERPs recorded in the MCN at CS+ onset did not show a statistically significant difference between EE and LE.
source: During extinction training, the peak-to-peak amplitude of the ERPs recorded in the MCN and vlPAG at CS+ onset did not show a statistically significant difference (Figure 3A and C; MCN: EE ERP 421.6 ± 126 mV vs. LE ERP 309.3 ± 88.7 mV, t(5) = 1.905, p=0.115, paired t-test
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of ERP amplitude data, with reference to Figures 3A and C.

claim: During extinction training, the peak-to-peak amplitude of the ERPs recorded in the vlPAG at CS+ onset did not show a statistically significant difference between EE and LE.
source: During extinction training, the peak-to-peak amplitude of the ERPs recorded in the MCN and vlPAG at CS+ onset did not show a statistically significant difference (Figure 3A and C; MCN: EE ERP 421.6 ± 126 mV vs. LE ERP 309.3 ± 88.7 mV, t(5) = 1.905, p=0.115, paired t-test; vlPAG: EE ERP 501.1.2 ± 104.7 mV vs. LE ERP 418 ± 84.08 mV, t(5) = 1.122, p=0.313, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of ERP amplitude data, with reference to Figures 3A and C.

claim: ERPs recorded at CS+ offset in the vlPAG showed a significant decrease in amplitude during extinction training (65% reduction from EE to LE).
source: By comparison, ERPs recorded at CS+ offset in the vlPAG (Figure 3B and D) showed a significant decrease in amplitude during extinction training in EE versus LE (65% reduction in ERP size, EE 520.3 ± 124.7 vs. LE 337.8 ± 96.29, t(5) = 2.258, p=0.007, paired t-test)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of ERP amplitude data, with reference to Figures 3B and D.

claim: ERPs recorded at CS+ offset in the MCN showed no significant decrease in amplitude during extinction training.
source: while in the MCN there was no significant decrease (EE 537.3 ± 173.2 vs. LE 430.5 ± 135.6, t(5) = 2.258, p=0.074, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of ERP amplitude data.

claim: The differences found in vlPAG between onset and offset ERPs provide further evidence that they are generated and regulated by different neural pathways.
source: The differences found in vlPAG between onset and offset ERPs provide further evidence that they are generated and regulated by different neural pathways.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed differences in ERP characteristics between onset and offset.

claim: There was a significant correlation between the amplitude of ERP responses recorded in MCN and vlPAG at CS+ onset (rrm = 0.64, p<0.0001).
source: There was a significant correlation between the amplitude of ERP responses recorded in MCN and vlPAG for all available cases (n = 6 animals) for both CS+ onset and CS+ offset (onset, rrm = 0.64, p<0.0001
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis using repeated-measures correlation.

claim: There was a significant correlation between the amplitude of ERP responses recorded in MCN and vlPAG at CS+ offset (rrm = 0.44, p=0.033).
source: There was a significant correlation between the amplitude of ERP responses recorded in MCN and vlPAG for all available cases (n = 6 animals) for both CS+ onset and CS+ offset (onset, rrm = 0.64, p<0.0001; offset, rrm = 0.44, p=0.033; repeated-measures correlation).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis using repeated-measures correlation.

claim: Population activity in MCN and vlPAG broadly parallels the changes that occur in vlPAG single-unit peak activity at onset and offset of the CS+ during extinction of a fear-conditioned response.
source: Taken together, these ERP data therefore suggest that population activity in MCN and vlPAG broadly parallels the changes that occur in vlPAG single-unit peak activity at onset and offset of the CS+ during extinction of a fear-conditioned response.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the ERP and single-unit data.

claim: Muscimol infusion into the MCN induced ataxia in all animals.
source: Immediately after the infusion all animals (n = 8 rats) displayed mild to moderate ataxia, providing a positive control that the muscimol was disrupting cerebellar activity.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral observations following muscimol infusion.

claim: The severity of muscimol-induced ataxia gradually reduced over several hours, and animals were behaviourally normal after 24 hr.
source: The severity of the ataxia gradually reduced over several hours, and the animals were behaviourally normal after 24 hr.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral observations following muscimol infusion.

claim: There was no significant difference between the overall firing rates of vlPAG units across habituation, acquisition, and extinction training in muscimol experiments.
source: There was no significant difference between the overall firing rates across habituation, acquisition, and extinction training (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, F(2, 49) = 0.506, p=0.079, n = 52, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of firing rate data, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In muscimol experiments, 71% (10/14 units) of type 1 onset units showed a reduction in responsiveness during extinction training as measured by mean change in integrated area of response.
source: Similar to the control results described above, the majority (71%, 10/14 units) of available type 1 onset units (Figure 2C) showed a reduction in responsiveness during extinction training as measured by mean change in integrated area of response (Figure 2D; on average, the integrated area of response was 77.8% smaller between EE and LE, t(9) = 4.294, p=0.002, n = 10, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of the experimental data from muscimol experiments, with reference to Figures 2C and D.

claim: In muscimol experiments, no significant difference was found for mean peak z-score of type 1 onset responses between EE and LE.
source: In keeping with the findings from control animals, no significant difference was found for mean peak z-score (Figure 2E, peak 0.7% smaller between EE and LE, t(9) = 1.707, p=0.122, n = 10, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of the experimental data from muscimol experiments, with reference to Figure 2E.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference between control and muscimol animals for type 1 CS+ onset responses in EE or LE for integrated area or peak z-score.
source: There was also no statistically significant difference between control and muscimol animals for type 1 CS+ onset responses in EE or LE for either measure of response (Figure 2D and E, for control n = 18 vs. muscimol n = 10; mean integrated area in EE, t(26) = 0.112, p=0.912, unpaired t-test; mean integrated area in LE, t(26) = 0.949, p=0.351, unpaired t-test; mean peak z-score in EE, t(26) = 0.103, p=0.919, unpaired t-test; mean peak z-score in LE, t(26) = 0.454, p=0.654, unpaired t-test)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and muscimol data, with reference to Figures 2D and E.

claim: There was no difference in overall firing rates for all units during extinction training between control and muscimol animals.
source: nor was there a difference in overall firing rates for all units during extinction training (control vs. muscimol; t(78) = 0.407, p=0.685, unpaired t-test; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and muscimol data, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: In muscimol experiments during EE, the mean integrated area of response at CS+ offset increased by 58.5% compared to control.
source: The mean integrated area of response in muscimol experiments increased by 58.5% by comparison to control (Figure 2H, for control n = 19 vs. muscimol n = 10, t(27) = 2.645, p=0.014, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and muscimol data, with reference to Figure 2H.

claim: In muscimol experiments during EE, the mean peak z-score at CS+ offset was 60% of control, but this was not statistically significant.
source: There was also a reduction in mean peak z-score at EE (Figure 2G, muscimol mean peak was 60% of control), but this was not statistically significant (Figure 2I, t(27) = 0.660, p=0.515, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and muscimol data, with reference to Figures 2G and 2I.

claim: In LE, muscimol experiments had a significantly increased area of response at CS+ offset compared to control animals (41.6% larger).
source: In LE, the mean integrated area of response was also significantly different. On average, muscimol experiments had a significantly increased area of response than control animals (41.6% larger, Figure 2H, t(27) = 2.365, p=0.014, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and muscimol data, with reference to Figure 2H.

claim: In LE, the mean peak z-score at CS+ offset was not significantly different between muscimol and control experiments.
source: Similar to CS+ onset, the mean peak z-score in LE was not significantly different between muscimol and control experiments (Figure 2I, t(27) = 1.013, p=0.32, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and muscimol data, with reference to Figure 2I.

claim: After CS+ onset, there was no significant difference in total number of peaks between muscimol and control animals in EE or LE.
source: After CS+ onset, there was no significant difference in total number of peaks between muscimol and control animals (Figure 4A; EE, t(36) = 1.570, p=0.125; LE, t(37) = 0.651, p=0.519; unpaired t-test)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and muscimol data, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: After CS+ onset, there was no significant difference in latency to peak between muscimol and control animals.
source: nor latency to peak (Figure 4B; χ2(4) = 2.50, p=0.645, chi-square), with both groups having about 85% of peaks occurring in the 200 ms immediately following CS+ onset.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and muscimol data, with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Following CS+ offset, both the number and latency of peaks significantly increased during EE in muscimol animals compared to controls.
source: By contrast, following CS+ offset both the number (Figure 4C; t(31) = 7.184, p<0.0001 unpaired t-test) and latency (Figure 4D; χ2(4) = 13.31, p<0.01, chi-square) of peaks significantly increased during EE in muscimol animals.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and muscimol data, with reference to Figures 4C and D.

claim: In LE, there was no increase in the number of peaks following CS+ offset in muscimol animals compared to controls.
source: In LE, there was no increase in the number of peaks (t(22) = 0.019, p=0.98).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and muscimol data in LE.

claim: In control animals, 82% of peaks following CS+ offset occurred in the 200 ms immediately following the CS+ offset.
source: In control animals, 82% of peaks occurred in the 200 ms immediately following the CS+ offset
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis.

claim: In muscimol animals, only 20% of peaks following CS+ offset occurred in the 200 ms immediately following the CS+ offset.
source: while only 20% of muscimol animals had peaks during the same time period.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data analysis.

claim: During extinction training, the pattern of response of vlPAG units at CS+ onset is mainly unaffected by pharmacological block of MCN during consolidation.
source: Taken all together, these data therefore suggest that during extinction training the pattern of response of vlPAG units at CS+ onset is mainly unaffected by pharmacological block of MCN during consolidation
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the comparison of control and muscimol data for CS+ onset responses.

claim: The temporally precise activity at CS+ offset is disrupted during EE by pharmacological block of MCN during consolidation.
source: but the temporally precise activity at CS+ offset is disrupted during EE, providing additional evidence that the two responses are independent of one another.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the comparison of control and muscimol data for CS+ offset responses.

claim: Both control and muscimol animals showed extinction of the conditioned freezing response during presentation of the CS+ between EE and LE.
source: During presentation of the CS+, both control and muscimol animals showed extinction of the conditioned freezing response between EE vs. LE (Figure 5A; control, EE freezing = 74.11% ± 3.7% vs. LE freezing = 31.1% ± 7.2%, t(9) = 9.730, p<0.0001, n = 10 animals; muscimol, EE freezing = 74.17% ± 6.1% vs. LE freezing = 36.0% ± 10.7%, t(7) = 5.404, p=0.001, n = 8 animals; paired t-tests
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of freezing behavior data, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: No significant differences were detected between control and muscimol animals in the percentage of time freezing during CS+ presentation in EE or LE.
source: No significant differences were detected between control and muscimol animals in the percentage of time freezing during EE or LE (Figure 5A; EE, t(16) = 0.0091, p=0.9928; LE, t(16) = 0.3937, p=0.579; unpaired t-test)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and muscimol freezing behavior, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: There was no difference detected in rate of extinction of freezing during CS+ presentation between control and muscimol animals.
source: nor was there a difference detected in rate of extinction of freezing (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A; control, –1.6 ± 1.9; muscimol, –2.4 ± 1.2; t(16) = 1.00, p=0.332, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and muscimol extinction rates, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Both control and muscimol animals showed extinction of freezing during the ITI between EE and LE.
source: In terms of freezing behaviour during the ITI, both control and muscimol animals showed extinction learning similar to that found during presentation of the CS+ (Figure 5B; EE vs. LE: control, t(9) = 6.881, p<0.0001; muscimol, t(7) = 3.952, p=0.006, paired t-tests
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of freezing behavior during ITI, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: There was no significant difference in muscimol animals compared to controls for percentage of time freezing during ITI in either EE or LE.
source: There was no significant difference in muscimol animals by comparison to controls for either EE or LE (Figure 5D; EE, t(16) = 0.048, p=0.963; LE, t(16) = 0.902, p=0.929; unpaired t-tests).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing control and muscimol freezing during ITI, with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: There was no significant difference in the rate of extinction during ITI between control and muscimol groups.
source: Nor was there a significant difference in the rate of extinction between groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B; t(16) = 0.336, p=0.742, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing extinction rates during ITI, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There was no difference in the duration of freezing or movement epochs between control and muscimol animals at baseline.
source: For baseline behaviour monitored just before extinction training (see Materials and methods), there was no difference in the duration of freezing or movement epochs between control and muscimol animals (freezing duration for control 3.1 (1.6, 6.5) s, median ± interquartile range [IQR], n = 8 and muscimol 4.5 (3.6, 14.7) s, median ± IQR, n = 8, U = 19, p=0.195, Mann–Whitney test; movement duration for control 7.3 (3.5,14.8) s, median ± IQR, n = 10, and muscimol 7.7 (1.7, 27.12) s, median ± IQR, n = 8, U = 38, p=0.877, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of baseline behavior.

claim: Upon presentation of the CS+, there was a significant increase in the duration of freezing epochs in muscimol compared with control animals in both EE and LE.
source: However, upon presentation of the CS+, there was a significant increase in the duration of freezing epochs in muscimol compared with control animals in both EE and LE (Figure 5C; EE: control 9.2 (2.8, 14.7) s, median ± IQR, n = 10; muscimol 26.45 (14.5, 82.2) s, median ± IQR, n = 8, U = 13, p=0.014, Mann–Whitney test; LE: control 3.4 (2.3, 7.0) s, median ± IQR, n = 9; muscimol 9.1 (5.6, 23.5) s, median ± IQR, n = 8, U = 13, p=0.026, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing freezing epoch duration, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: There was a significant increase in movement epochs in EE in muscimol compared to control animals.
source: There was also a significant increase in movement epochs in EE in muscimol by comparison to control animals, but there was no significant difference in LE (Figure 5D; EE: control 1.6 (1.4, 2.0) s, median ± IQR, n = 10; muscimol 4.09 (2.4, 6.8) s, median ± IQR, n = 8, U = 8, p=0.003, Mann–Whitney test
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing movement epoch duration, with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: There was no significant difference in movement epochs in LE between muscimol and control animals.
source: but there was no significant difference in LE (Figure 5D; EE: control 1.6 (1.4, 2.0) s, median ± IQR, n = 10; muscimol 4.09 (2.4, 6.8) s, median ± IQR, n = 8, U = 8, p=0.003, Mann–Whitney test; LE: control 4 (2.1, 11.0) s, median ± IQR, n = 10; muscimol 8.5 (3.0, 16.02) s, median ± IQR, n = 8, U = 29, p=0.36, Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis comparing movement epoch duration, with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: From EE to LE, the duration of freezing epochs significantly decreased in both control and muscimol animals.
source: As might be expected during extinction training, from EE to LE the duration of freezing epochs significantly decreased in both control and muscimol animals (Figure 5C; control, p=0.039; muscimol, p=0.008, Wilcoxon test)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of freezing epoch duration over extinction, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: From EE to LE, there was a corresponding increase in the duration of movement epochs that was statistically significant for controls but not for muscimol-treated animals.
source: and there was a corresponding increase in the duration of movement epochs. However, the latter difference was statistically significant for controls (Figure 5D; p=0.033, Wilcoxon test) but not for muscimol-treated animals (p=0.250, Wilcoxon test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of movement epoch duration over extinction, with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: Blocking MCN activity during consolidation does not alter the overall proportion of time spent freezing during subsequent extinction training, but does increase the duration of individual freezing bouts.
source: Taken altogether, these results therefore indicate that blocking MCN activity during consolidation does not alter the overall proportion of time spent freezing during subsequent extinction training, but does increase the duration of individual freezing bouts, that is, freezing bouts are longer but fewer in number as there are also longer bouts of movement.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the behavioral data comparing control and muscimol animals.

claim: At CS+ onset, there was a significant positive correlation between unit response and percentage time spent freezing for individual animals in both control and muscimol groups.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Ozawa et al., 2016; Wright and McDannald, 2019), at CS+ onset there was a significant positive correlation in both control and muscimol groups between unit response and percentage time spent freezing for individual animals (Figure 5E; control, rrm = 0.38, p=0.048, n = 7 animals; muscimol, rrm = 0.58, p=0.038, n = 3 animals; repeated-measures correlation).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis using repeated-measures correlation, with reference to Figure 5E and citations to previous research.

claim: A significant positive correlation was present between unit response at CS+ offset and percentage time spent freezing during ITI for both control and muscimol animals.
source: A significant positive correlation was also present between unit response at CS+ offset and percentage time spent freezing during ITI for both control and muscimol animals (Figure 5F; control, rrm = 0.55, p=0.002, n = 7 animals; muscimol, rrm = 0.69, p=0.008, n = 3 animals; repeated-measures correlation).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis using repeated-measures correlation, with reference to Figure 5F.

claim: No significant relationship was found between the absolute change in freezing for each animal and the mean absolute change in unit response during extinction training.
source: To investigate whether the extent of change in freezing behaviour and unit response during extinction training were related, a comparison was made between the absolute change in freezing for each animal with the mean absolute change in unit response. No significant relationship was found between freezing and unit response area at CS+ onset, nor for freezing during the ITI and unit response area at CS+ offset (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: The magnitude of vlPAG unit responses at both onset and offset of a conditioned tone reflects general fear state within an individual animal, but does not predict which individuals will have a stronger freezing response overall.
source: Taken together, these results therefore suggest that the magnitude of vlPAG unit responses at both onset and offset of a conditioned tone reflects general fear state within an individual animal, but does not predict which individuals will have a stronger freezing response overall.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the correlation analyses between unit responses and freezing behavior.

claim: By comparison to controls, no statistically significant effects were observed in rearing activity during extinction training in muscimol animals.
source: To investigate whether MCN inactivation during consolidation had an effect on other defence-related behaviours, rearing activity and USVs were monitored during presentation of the CS+ and ITI during extinction training. However, by comparison to controls, no statistically significant effects were observed in either type of behaviour in muscimol animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of rearing behavior, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2E–H.

claim: By comparison to controls, no statistically significant effects were observed in USVs during extinction training in muscimol animals.
source: To investigate whether MCN inactivation during consolidation had an effect on other defence-related behaviours, rearing activity and USVs were monitored during presentation of the CS+ and ITI during extinction training. However, by comparison to controls, no statistically significant effects were observed in either type of behaviour in muscimol animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of USV behavior, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2E–H.

claim: A direct anatomical connection exists between MCN and vlPAG, with terminal projections in the PAG primarily localised to its ventrolateral region on the contralateral side.
source: As a first step, a direct anatomical connection was investigated by injecting a fluorescently tagged anterograde virus into the MCN (n = 7 rats, Figure 6—figure supplement 1). In every case, terminal projections in the PAG were primarily localised to its ventrolateral region on the contralateral side.
evidence: This is a direct report of anatomical tracing experiments, with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Double-labelled neurons in MCN (projecting to PAG and transfected with DREADD) represented on average 70% ± 10.2% when expressed relative to the PAG-labelled population.
source: Double-labelled neurons in MCN represented on average 70% ± 10.2% and 28% ± 8.3 when expressed relative to the PAG and DREADD single-labelled populations, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: This is a direct report of anatomical quantification, with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: Double-labelled neurons in MCN represented on average 28% ± 8.3 when expressed relative to the DREADD-labelled population.
source: Double-labelled neurons in MCN represented on average 70% ± 10.2% and 28% ± 8.3 when expressed relative to the PAG and DREADD single-labelled populations, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: This is a direct report of anatomical quantification, with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: MCN-PAG projection neurons were likely to be transfected with DREADD in the experiments.
source: These anatomical results therefore suggest that MCN-PAG projection neurons were likely to be transfected with DREADD in our experiments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the anatomical double-labelling data.

claim: During acquisition, there was no significant difference in the percentage of freezing between control versus DREADD animals during CS-US paired presentations.
source: During acquisition, there was no significant difference in the percentage of freezing between control versus DREADD animals during CS-US paired presentations (Figure 6B, upper panel, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA; time, F(4.45, 75.64) = 16.63, p<0.0001; virus, F(1, 17) = 0.089, p=0.769)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of freezing behavior during acquisition, with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: During acquisition, there was no significant difference in the percentage of freezing between control versus DREADD animals during the ITI.
source: nor during the ITI (Figure 6B, lower panel, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA; time, F(3.834, 65.19) = 17.82, p<0.0001; virus, F(1, 17) = 2.339, p=0.144).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of freezing behavior during ITI in acquisition, with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: During the ITI in acquisition, there was a significant reduction (36%) in the number of USVs in DREADD animals compared to controls.
source: However, comparison of the mean total number of USVs per animal in DREADD versus control groups across all acquisition trials showed that during the ITI there was a significant reduction in the number of USVs (Figure 6C, lower panel, a decrease of 36%, control 34 (0.0 201.5) s, median ± IQR, DREADD 0 (0.0 29.25) s, median ± IQR, U = 23, p=0.032, Mann–Whitney test, one-tailed).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of USV behavior during ITI in acquisition, with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: During CS-US presentations in acquisition, there was no significant difference in the number of USVs between DREADD and control animals.
source: This difference was not apparent during CS-US presentations (Figure 6C, upper panel, control 0 (0.0 10.0) s, median ± IQR, DREADD 0 (0.0 4.5) s, median ± IQR, U = 39, p=0.310, Mann–Whitney test, one-tailed).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of USV behavior during CS-US presentations in acquisition, with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: During extinction training, control and DREADD animals showed similar levels of freezing during presentation of the CS+ in EE and LE.
source: During extinction training, control and DREADD animals showed similar levels of freezing during presentation of the CS+ (Figure 7A; EE t(17) = 0.469, p=0.645, LE t(17) = 0.937, p=0.362, unpaired t-test)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of freezing behavior during extinction, with reference to Figure 7A.

claim: During extinction training, control and DREADD animals showed similar levels of freezing during the ITI in EE and LE.
source: and the ITI (Figure 7B; EE t(17) = 0.687, p=0.501, LE t(17) = 0.822, p=0.422, unpaired t-test)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of freezing behavior during ITI in extinction, with reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Both control and DREADD groups showed similar levels of extinction learning during CS+ presentation.
source: Both groups also showed similar levels of extinction learning during CS+ (control, t(8) = 3.335, p=0.010; DREADD, t(9) = 10.31, p<0.0001, paired t-test)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of extinction learning during CS+ presentation.

claim: Both control and DREADD groups showed similar levels of extinction learning during the ITI.
source: and the ITI (control, t(8) = 3.950, p=0.004; DREADD, t(9) = 8.679, p<0.0001, paired t-tests).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of extinction learning during ITI.

claim: The rate of extinction during the CS+ was significantly slower in DREADD animals compared to controls.
source: However, the rate of extinction during the CS+ was significantly slower in DREADD animals (Figure 7C; t(17) = 2.2.01, p=0.042, unpaired t-test)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of extinction rate during CS+ presentation, with reference to Figure 7C.

claim: The rate of extinction during the ITI was not significantly different between DREADD and control animals.
source: but not during the ITI (Figure 7D; t(17) = 1.096, p=0.229, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of extinction rate during ITI, with reference to Figure 7D.

claim: The finding that extinction rate during ITI was not affected suggests that the effect on CS+ extinction is not a general disruption of the expression of freezing behaviour.
source: The latter finding suggests that the effect is not a general disruption of the expression of freezing behaviour.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects on extinction rate during CS+ versus ITI.

claim: No differences in rearing behaviour were found between control and DREADD animals during extinction training.
source: With regard to rearing behaviour, no differences were found between control and DREADD animals both within EE and LE (Figure 7E and F; EE CS+, t(17) = 1.058, p=0.305; EE ITI, t(17) = 0.124, p=0.903; LE CS+, t(17) = 1.134, p=0.273; LE ITI, t(17) = 0.276, p=0.786, unpaired t-test), nor across all extinction training (Figure 7E and F; EE vs. LE; control CS+, t(8) = 0.610, p=0.556, control ITI, t(8) = 1.189, p=0.269; DREADD, CS+ t(9) = 1.246, p=0.244; DREADD, ITI, t(9) = 1.765, p=0.111, paired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of rearing behavior during extinction, with reference to Figures 7E and F.

claim: There was no significant difference in the total number of USVs per animal in DREADD versus control groups across all extinction training.
source: Similarly, there was also no significant difference in the total number of USVs per animal in DREADD versus control groups across all extinction training (Figure 7G and H; CS+, control 0 (0.0 4.5) s, median ± IQR, DREADD 0 (0.0 9.5) s, median ± IQR, U = 42.5, p=0.844; ITI, control 0 (0.0 73.0) s, median ± IQR, DREADD 0 (5.5 56.75) s, median ± IQR, U = 42.5, p=0.849, Mann–Whitney tests
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of USV behavior during extinction, with reference to Figures 7G and H.

claim: By comparison to controls, no statistically significant difference was found in anxiety and motor behaviour tests (elevated plus maze, open field, beam walking) following CNO infusion into vlPAG in DREADD animals.
source: To test for potential changes in anxiety and motor behaviour induced by modulation of the MCN-PAG pathway, the same DREADD and control animals studied in the fear conditioning experiments (n = 18 rats) were also tested on the following tasks after CNO infusion into vlPAG: elevated plus maze, open field, and beam walking. By comparison to controls, no statistically significant difference was found in any of these behaviours (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–E)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of control behavioral tests, with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: No evidence was obtained to suggest that targeted modulation of the MCN-PAG pathway causes a general deficit in motor behaviour or a change in anxiety levels.
source: Thus, no evidence was obtained to suggest that targeted modulation of the MCN-PAG pathway causes a general deficit in motor behaviour, nor a change in anxiety levels.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the control behavioral test results.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of CNO produced ataxia in every DREADD case, although this was generally less severe and shorter lasting (~1 hr) than observed in muscimol animals.
source: In all available animals (controls, n = 8; DREADD, n = 9), we therefore made an intraperitoneal injection of CNO in order to test for non-specific effects, including general action on MCN and its projections. Consistent with the muscimol experiments, in every DREADD case, the CNO produced ataxia, although this was generally less severe and shorter lasting (~1 hr) than was observed in the muscimol animals.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral observations following CNO injection.

claim: DREADD animals were significantly slower than control animals at traversing the beam following intraperitoneal CNO injection.
source: Impairments in motor behaviour were assessed by testing the animals on the beam walking task; DREADD animals were significantly slower than control animals at traversing the beam (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F, t(16) = 3.192, p=0.006, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of beam walking performance following CNO injection, with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2F.

claim: vlPAG neurons encode temporally precise information about both the onset and offset of a fear-conditioned auditory stimulus.
source: We have shown that vlPAG neurons (type 1 units) encode temporally precise information about both the onset and offset of a fear-conditioned auditory stimulus and that these two neuronal signals may be generated by independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data presented in the Results section.

claim: vlPAG neuronal signals for CS+ onset and offset may be generated by independent mechanisms.
source: We have shown that vlPAG neurons (type 1 units) encode temporally precise information about both the onset and offset of a fear-conditioned auditory stimulus and that these two neuronal signals may be generated by independent mechanisms.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence presented in the Results section.

claim: vlPAG units displayed little or no response to an auditory tone during habituation but displayed robust activity at tone onset and/or offset when the same tone was classically conditioned.
source: Importantly, vlPAG units displayed little or no response to an auditory tone during habituation but displayed robust activity at tone onset and/or offset when the same tone was classically conditioned.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental observations comparing habituation and conditioning phases.

claim: The vlPAG responses to conditioned tone were related to the associative conditioning rather than the sensory stimulus.
source: This provides evidence that the responses were related to the associative conditioning rather than the sensory stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that responses emerged after conditioning but not during habituation.

claim: Disruption of the temporal precision of the conditioned tone offset neural response following MCN inactivation during consolidation suggests a role of the cerebellum in the subsequent timing, but not the generation, of the vlPAG offset response.
source: Moreover, disruption of the temporal precision of the conditioned tone offset neural response following MCN inactivation during consolidation suggests a role of the cerebellum in the subsequent timing, but not the generation, of the vlPAG offset response.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the muscimol inactivation experiments showing altered temporal characteristics but not complete abolition of offset responses.

claim: The possibility remains that at other times during conditioning (acquisition and/or retrieval) the cerebellum is also involved in generating the response in vlPAG.
source: However, the possibility remains that at other times during conditioning (acquisition and/or retrieval) the cerebellum is also involved in generating the response in vlPAG, but this requires further study.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging limitations of the current study.

claim: Previous inactivation studies in rats using TTX have indicated that the cerebellar vermal cortex is involved in the consolidation of associatively conditioned cue and context-dependent fear memories.
source: Previous inactivation studies in rats using TTX have indicated that the cerebellar vermal cortex is involved in the consolidation of associatively conditioned cue and context-dependent fear memories (Sacchetti et al., 2002; Sacchetti et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The vermal compartment of the cerebellum is involved in various aspects of fear learning.
source: This suggests that the vermal compartment of the cerebellum is involved in various aspects of fear learning.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from previous research findings cited.

claim: The finding that inactivation of MCN leads to deficits in both USVs and freezing behaviour strongly supports the multiplicity of function of the vermal compartment in fear learning.
source: The finding in the present study that inactivation of a major output of the vermal compartment, MCN, leads to deficits in both USVs and freezing behaviour strongly supports this multiplicity of function.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion drawn from the current experimental findings in relation to previous research.

claim: In mice, inactivation of the MCN-PAG pathway during acquisition but not consolidation reduced the subsequent rate of extinction of conditioned freezing behaviour during retrieval.
source: The present results are also consistent with Frontera et al., 2020, who found in mice that inactivation of the MCN-PAG pathway during acquisition but not consolidation reduced the subsequent rate of extinction of conditioned freezing behaviour during retrieval.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research in mice.

claim: DREADD-induced modulation of the MCN-PAG pathway during acquisition slowed subsequent extinction rate in rats.
source: The present experiments in rats found that DREADD-induced modulation of the MCN-PAG pathway during acquisition slowed subsequent extinction rate
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental findings from the DREADD experiments.

claim: Muscimol inactivation of MCN during consolidation had no detectable effect on the proportion of time spent freezing during extinction.
source: while muscimol inactivation during consolidation had no detectable effect on freezing behaviour (suggesting comparability across species).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental findings from the muscimol experiments.

source: The reliability of this prediction is reduced with successive presentations of the unreinforced CS+.

source: If fear extinction is instructed by this error signal, then neurons encoding prediction errors would be expected to progressively decrease their CS+-induced firing rate upon repeated omission of the expected US (McNally et al., 2011).
